title: Apple TV Buys an Existing Hit for the First Time Ever
content:
Apple TV has bought the worldwide rights to "Small Prophets," breaking with how it normally operates in acquiring an existing English-language hit rather than commissioning a show of its own from the start.



‌Apple TV‌ has typically developed or, at the very least, commissioned shows in-house and given them their premiere on the service, regardless of where they may eventually end up. This was the model behind the BBC's "Trying," which ‌Apple TV‌+ produced first and later licensed to the BBC once its own run had finished.

Apple has also picked up individual foreign-language titles in the past, such as the French-Japanese drama "Drops of God." "Small Prophets" marks new ground since it is an English-language series and it had already become a broadcast hit elsewhere before Apple stepped in.

Deadline, follows a run on BBC Two that produced the strongest 28-day launch numbers for a comedy on the channel since 2022, a 100% score on Rotten Tomatoes, and the International Panorama award at this year's Series Mania festival.

"Small Prophets" will stream on ‌Apple TV‌ worldwide starting on October 7, with the exception of the UK, where the show debuted on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two earlier this year. Viewers in the UK will be able to continue watching it on iPlayer before it eventually moves to ‌Apple TV‌.

The show is written, created, and directed by Mackenzie Crook, best known for appearing in "The Office" and "The Detectorists."

Small Prophets follows Quigley as the eccentric Michael Sleep, an ordinary man who, since his darling Clea disappeared seven years ago, has worked in a DIY store, while visiting his elderly dad Brian and hoping for Clea to return. One day, Brian shares an old recipe for a potion so a skeptical Michael can create homunculi – magical spirits that can predict the future – to learn if he will see Clea again.

Michael gets help from his young DIY store co-worker Kacey and their unlikely friendship blossoms through a dislike of store manager Gordon, while his nosy neighbors obsess about what Michael is doing in the garden shed.



Deadline compared "Small Prophets" to "Ted Lasso," which recently began its fourth season as ‌Apple TV‌'s biggest premiere ever, favoring a gentler, more serialized storytelling style over a traditional sitcom.

title: iPhone 18 Pro Pre-Orders May Start at an Unusual Time
content:
Pre-orders of Apple's iPhone 18 Pro may not open until Saturday, September 12, a day later than the company's usual schedule, according to a new report.


Apple is set to hold its annual iPhone event on Wednesday, September 9, where the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ models, its first-ever foldable iPhone, and the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are all expected to be announced. 

Macworld reports that its German sister publication, Macwelt, has heard from a reliable source that Apple will instead push pre-orders back to Saturday, September 12.

There is precedent for this as the shift is reportedly tied to the date itself. September 11, 2026 marks the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, and Apple has moved pre-orders away from that date before. In 2015, when the standard pre-order Friday also landed on September 11, Apple delayed iPhone 6S and 6S Plus pre-orders to Saturday, September 12.

The timing within the day is also said to be changing. Apple's pre-orders traditionally open at 5 a.m. PT, but the source says this year's window will instead start at midnight PT on Saturday.

The delayed pre-order date is expected to apply to the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌, Apple Watch Series 12, and Apple Watch Ultra 4, alongside any other hardware Apple introduces at the event. Apple's foldable iPhone could follow at a later date, with pre-orders potentially not opening until late September.

Macwelt reported that Apple would announce the iPhone 17e on Thursday, February 19, but that announcement didn't actually come until March 2. That being said, Saturday, September 12 looks like a solid bet for the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌'s pre-order date, though the reported midnight PT start time is worth taking with a pinch of salt for now. Apple's iPhone event takes place in just under two weeks, on September 9.

title: What NOT to Expect at Apple's 'Surprise and Shine' September 9 Event
content:
Apple's annual fall event takes place on Wednesday, September 9, when it is expected to unveil new iPhone 18 Pro models, the first foldable iPhone, an Apple Watch Series 12, a fourth-generation Apple Watch Ultra, and potentially AirPods 5. Apple may also make some additional new products available at its "Surprise and shine" event, but there are a handful of rumored upcoming devices that we don't expect to make an appearance this month.


To help set expectations ahead of Apple's "Surprise and shine" event, here are the products that Apple is unlikely to announce in September, but rather later on in the year or in 2027.

iPhone 18


reported split-launch strategy. Going forward, Apple will dedicate its annual September event to its more expensive Pro-model iPhones and successive generations of its upcoming foldable iPhone.

9GB of RAM, 1GB more than the iPhone 17, while analyst Jeff Pu believes Apple will upgrade it with 12GB. If the iPhone 18 is limited to 9GB RAM, it will not support all Apple Intelligence features.

24-megapixel front-facing camera, up from 18 megapixels. There are reports that Apple will use an improved display, which could also feature a smaller Dynamic Island.

iPhone Air 2


The iPhone Air that came out in September 2025 alongside the iPhone 17 lineup didn't sell as well as expected, and a second version is no longer believed to be coming in September 2026. Despite some debate about the future of the iPhone Air, the latest rumors suggest a new model is still in development, and will likely arrive in spring 2027 alongside the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e.

second camera to the next iPhone Air to make it more appealing to consumers and to justify its $999 starting price. Apple also wants to improve battery life, either through an increased battery size or improvements to efficiency. Given that the design of the new model is similar to the current design, there may not be room for a larger battery. The device will use an A20 Pro chip built on Apple's new 2nm process, so it could feature better efficiency.

New Apple Watch SE 4


The current Apple Watch SE 3 is Apple's most affordable Apple Watch option. Apple updated it in September 2025, but we are not expecting a new model in 2026, and there's no word yet on when a new version is coming.

New Macs


updated 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M6 chip in late 2026, followed by a major high-end MacBook Pro redesign in late 2026 or early 2027. Reportedly dubbed "MacBook Ultra," the new 14-inch and 16-inch models are expected to feature M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, an OLED display, a touch screen, a Dynamic Island, and a thinner design.

While it isn't impossible, we're unlikely to see any Macs debut on September 9. Apple typically uses its fall event to focus on new iPhone and Apple Watch models. The company usually unveils new Macs in October via press release or a separate event. 

Possibly, Maybe

In addition to new iPhone 18 Pro models, Apple Watch models, and AirPods, Apple is expected to prepare other products for release this year. title: Apple TV just got another price increase
content:
Macworld





Apple TV has been on a bit of a roll lately, with a string of hit shows including Widow’s Bay, Severance, Pluribus, and the return of Ted Lasso. Unfortunately, all that premium programming doesn’t come cheaply, because Apple is raising prices on its streaming service once again, from $12.99 to $14.99 a month.
The last Apple TV price increase was a year ago when it raised prices from $9.99 to $12.99, a 30 percent price hike. This latest bump is about half that, but it’s still another financial pain point for Apple customers that already had to endure raising prices on most things Apple sells. Just this week, Apple introduced the M6 Mac mini starting at $899, 50 percent higher than a comparable model would have cost just a couple of months ago, and analysts are predicting higher prices on next month’s iPhones as well.
In response, the Apple One Individual bundle is also going up in price, from $19.95 per month to $21.95. Subscribers get access to Apple TV, Music, and Arcade, as well as 500GB of iCloud storage. The other Apple One plans, Family and Premier, which saw $2 increases in July, are unchanged.
Apple also raised prices on its Music streaming service in July by as much as $3 a month, depending on the tier.
When Apple TV launched in 2019 it cost just $4.99 a month with a one year free trial for anyone who purchased an eligible Apple product. Apple has since raised prices four times.

title: Do Macs need Antivirus in 2026? Is Apple’s security enough?
content:
Macworld





Macs include strong built-in malware protection, including XProtect, Gatekeeper, Notarization and other security layers, so third-party antivirus isn’t essential for everyone. If you keep macOS up to date, download apps only from the Mac App Store and trusted websites, and are cautious about links, attachments and unexpected prompts, Apple’s own protections may be sufficient.
However, macOS is not immune to threats. As Macs have become more popular, they’ve become a more attractive target for attackers, while the nature of those threats has shifted away from traditional viruses towards phishing, fake updates, malicious downloads and scams designed to trick users into installing malware themselves.
Third-party antivirus can provide an additional layer of protection, particularly against malicious websites, suspicious downloads, phishing and emerging threats. It may be worth considering if you regularly download unfamiliar software, install apps from outside trusted sources, use torrents, handle sensitive business or personal data, share files with Windows users, or simply want stronger web protection than macOS provides on its own.
Below, we explain the security features already built into macOS, where their limitations lie, and who is most likely to benefit from installing antivirus software.

Stay safe online with unlimited VPN, up to $1 Million of Identity Protection coverage, and AI-powered Cybersecurity software all for no more than $11 per month on the highest tier plan!

At a glance: Do you need antivirus on your Mac?
You probably don’t need additional antivirus if:
You install software primarily from trusted developers
You keep macOS and browsers updated
You use strong passwords/passkeys and MFA
You pay attention to Gatekeeper and browser warnings
You should consider antivirus if:
You routinely install software from unfamiliar sources
You work with sensitive business or client data
You frequently exchange files with Windows users
You want additional phishing/web filtering
Less technical family members use the Mac
You want centralized security controls across multiple devices
Who should buy antivirus for Mac?
For many Mac users, Apple’s built-in security features, including XProtect, Gatekeeper and Notarization, provide sufficient protection, particularly if you keep macOS up to date, download apps only from trusted sources, and are cautious about links, attachments and unexpected prompts. However, third-party antivirus can provide an additional layer of protection against phishing, malicious websites and suspicious downloads, and may be worthwhile if you regularly install unfamiliar software, use torrents, handle sensitive data, share files with Windows users, or simply want stronger protection than macOS provides on its own.


Type of userScenariosRecommendation

Low-risk userOnly downloads from App Store and trusted devs, automatic macOS updates turned onApple’s built-in tools are probably sufficient
High-risk userDownloads from various sites and torrentsPaid antivirus is strongly recommended
Non-technical userOlder person who clicks links and downloads attachments or struggles to judge scamsAdditional protection is more worthwhile, especially if it guards against malicious sites and offers phishing and download protection – not merely malware scanning.
Unsupported MacMac no longer receives security updatesAntivirus can reduce some malware risk temporarily but it is not a substitute for a supported version of macOS, so our recommendation is to update the Mac. 
Business user Handles sensitive data and client data, shares files with Windows PCsPaid antivirus is recommended for an extra safety layer
User wanting extra featuresRequires VPN, password manager, phishing protectionPaid antivirus is worthwhile if it comes with appealing bundled features

 






Do Macs have built-in antivirus?

				
					

				
			
 
Yes. Macs include built-in antivirus and malware protection as part of macOS. Apple uses several layers of security that work automatically in the background, so you don’t need to install anything to get a basic level of protection.
The main protections include:
XProtect: This is Apple’s built-in antivirus engine. It checks apps against regularly updated definitions for known malware and can block malicious software before it runs. Apple updates XProtect automatically in the background, without requiring any action from you.
Gatekeeper and Notarization: Gatekeeper helps prevent untrusted software from running. It checks apps downloaded from the internet to make sure they come from an identified developer and, where applicable, have been notarized by Apple. Notarization means Apple has checked the software for known malicious content. Gatekeeper can warn you or block an app if it fails these checks.
Sandboxing and permissions: macOS limits what apps can access and modify, while privacy controls require apps to request permission before accessing sensitive data and hardware such as files, the camera and microphone. These protections can limit the damage malicious software is able to cause.
XProtect Remediator: This works in the background to detect and remove malware that may already be present on your Mac. It scans periodically and receives security updates independently of full macOS updates, allowing Apple to respond more quickly to new threats.
Hardware-level security: Apple silicon Macs include security features such as the Secure Enclave and hardware-backed encryption, which help protect sensitive information and make some types of attack more difficult.
Background security updates: Apple can deliver important security improvements separately from major macOS updates, helping Macs receive protection against newly discovered threats more quickly.
Protection in highly targeted cyberattacks: If you believe you are being personally targeted by a sophisticated cyberattack, Apple offers Lockdown Mode, which severely restricts certain apps, websites and features to reduce the Mac’s attack surface. It is intended for people at unusually high risk from attacks such as mercenary spyware, rather than as everyday malware protection.
macOS also includes other safeguards designed to reduce the risk of users being tricked into running malicious software. For example, newer versions of macOS can warn when potentially dangerous commands are pasted into Terminal.
Together, these protections provide a strong security baseline. For users who keep macOS up to date, download apps primarily from the Mac App Store or reputable developers, and are cautious about links and downloads, Apple’s built-in security may be all they need.
However, as good as these protections are, there have been occasions when malware has managed to infiltrate the Mac platform, and times when Apple hasn’t responded to a threat as quickly as Mac users might hope. If you want the very best protection from threats, therefore, consider adding a dedicated Mac security suite such as our top pick Intego One. You’ll find Intego in our roundup of the best antivirus for Mac, among other free and paid-for antivirus apps that might give you some peace of mind, including McAfee and Norton.
Get the best Mac antivirus: Intego ONE 


							


Can Macs get viruses?

				
					

				
			
Apple makes it hard for you to install an app that could be malicious.

Foundry




Yes. Macs can get viruses and other forms of malware. macOS includes strong built-in protections, but Macs are not immune, and many of today’s biggest threats rely on social engineering rather than traditional viruses.
A Surfshark analysis of malware detections between January and July 2026 found that Windows PCs faced roughly six times greater malware risk than Macs. Even so, macOS still accounted for eight percent of detections despite representing 34 percent of the user base. Phishing was also the third-biggest threat to Mac users.
One of the biggest current risks is infostealer malware, which targets passwords, browser data, authentication cookies, cryptocurrency wallets and other sensitive information. Examples include ClickLock Stealer, which uses a fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA to trick users into pasting a malicious Terminal command, and CrashStealer, which impersonates Apple’s crash reporting tool to target browsers, password managers and crypto wallets.
Other threats include Banshee Stealer, which targets browser and cryptocurrency data; PamStealer, spread through fake websites impersonating legitimate apps; and JSCoreRunner, distributed through a fake PDF converter that alters Chrome settings to redirect users to fraudulent search engines.
Attackers are increasingly trying to bypass macOS protections by persuading users to approve malicious actions themselves. Apple has responded by adding warnings in macOS when potentially dangerous commands are pasted into Terminal.
The key point is that while traditional Mac viruses remain relatively uncommon, phishing, fake apps, malicious downloads and credential-stealing malware are real risks that Apple’s built-in tools cannot always prevent.


						

							


How can I tell if my Mac has malware?
Here are the key signs that your Mac may be infected with malware:
Your Mac runs hot, is very slow, and the fans are loud when the computer is idle.
Your usual home page has changed, you’re seeing redirects, extensions you didn’t install, or suspicious pop-ups — especially ones claiming “Your Mac is infected.”
Apps you don’t remember installing appear in your Applications folder or Dock.
You are seeing excessive CPU usage in Activity Monitor when your Mac should be idle.
Read: What to do if you think your Mac has a virus and How to tell if your Mac has been hacked – Key signs & what to do for more advice. 
Users who believe they may be targeted by spyware should also consider Apple’s Lockdown Mode. This dramatically restricts certain Mac features to reduce the attack surface, but it is intended for the small number of people at unusually high risk rather than everyday Mac users.


						

							


Is Apple’s built-in protection enough?
The answer depends heavily on how you use your Mac.
Apple’s security tools are effective at blocking known malware, but one of their biggest limitations is social engineering. Attackers increasingly try to persuade users to reveal passwords, visit malicious websites, or install software themselves.
Apple’s safeguards are not infallible either. Malware has occasionally been distributed using apparently legitimate developer credentials, while vulnerabilities have sometimes allowed attackers to bypass protections such as Gatekeeper before Apple could issue a fix.
For careful users, macOS’s built-in security may be sufficient. However, a reputable antivirus with strong phishing and web protection can provide a useful additional safety net.


						

							




Here’s how XProtect compares to traditional third-party antivirus software:


FeatureXProtect and other macOS security featuresThird-party antivirus

How it worksScans apps when first launched, when updated, or when the developer’s signature changesTypically offers continuous, real-time monitoring of file activity
Update frequencyUpdated regularly by Apple in the background, but definitions may lag behind emerging threatsOften updates virus definitions several times a day for faster response to new malware
Threat coverageFocuses primarily on known macOS malwareCovers a wider range including adware, spyware, trojans, ransomware, and cross-platform threats
Additional featuresXProtect includes malware scanning and removal. Safari provides warnings for suspected fraudulent websitesOften includes phishing protection, firewalls, VPNs, password managers, parental controls, and dark web monitoring
Performance impactNegligible, as it’s integrated into the OSVaries; some suites can cause system slowdowns

 






When is third-party antivirus worth installing?
Third-party antivirus is most worthwhile when your risk is higher than that of the average Mac user, or when you want protection that goes beyond what macOS provides on its own.
You should consider installing antivirus if you regularly download software from unfamiliar websites, install apps from outside the Mac App Store, use torrents, exchange files with Windows users, or handle sensitive business, financial or client data. It can also be particularly useful on a Mac used by less technical family members who may be more likely to click suspicious links, open unexpected attachments or respond to convincing scams.
A Mac can also potentially store or forward Windows malware without being affected by it itself, so antivirus can be useful in workplaces or households where files are regularly exchanged with Windows PCs.
Another good reason to install antivirus is stronger web and phishing protection. Many modern Mac threats rely on social engineering rather than exploiting macOS directly, using fake websites, malicious downloads or instructions that persuade users to install malware themselves. A good security suite can identify and block some of these threats before they reach your Mac.
Antivirus can also make sense if you want additional security features such as ransomware protection, identity monitoring, a VPN, parental controls or centralized protection across several Macs, PCs and mobile devices.
However, antivirus should complement rather than replace Apple’s security features and good security habits. If your Mac no longer receives macOS security updates, installing antivirus may reduce some risks, but upgrading to a Mac that can run a supported version of macOS is a much better long-term solution.


						

							


What do third-party antivirus solutions add?
macOS includes strong built-in protections, but third-party antivirus solutions can fill some gaps that Apple’s tools don’t fully address. If XProtect is a lock on your Mac’s front door, a paid antivirus solution acts more like an alarm system with security cameras.

				
					

				
			
Third-party antivirus, such as Intego One, add broader protection, controls, monitoring, privacy, and extras.

Foundry




Paid antivirus suites can offer features that go beyond what Apple offers or aren’t features of macOS, such as: 
Broader Threat Coverage: Apple’s XProtect and Gatekeeper primarily focus on known malware and verifying app signatures. Third-party tools go further by protecting against adware, spyware, trojans, ransomware, and phishing attempts that Apple’s systems may miss.
Real-Time Web and Phishing Protection: Safari includes built-in warnings for suspected fraudulent websites, but third-party security suites can extend web and phishing protection across browsers and may use additional threat databases to identify malicious sites, scam links and suspicious downloads.
More Frequent Updates: Apple updates XProtect signatures automatically and independently of macOS updates. Third-party antivirus vendors may update their detection systems more frequently or use cloud-based threat intelligence to respond quickly to emerging threats.
On-Demand and Scheduled Scanning: macOS scans apps automatically at launch, but you can’t force a manual scan. Third-party tools let you run quick scans, full system scans, and schedule regular checkups.
Ransomware protection: Some Mac antivirus apps protect important files and folders from unauthorized changes or encryption, preventing untrusted apps from modifying them. Some also protect Time Machine backups so clean copies remain available for recovery.
More advanced firewall controls: macOS includes a built-in firewall that can block unwanted incoming connections and restrict incoming access for individual apps. Some third-party security suites add more granular controls, including monitoring and blocking outgoing connections, alerts when apps attempt to access the network, network activity monitoring and intrusion-prevention features. 
VPN services: Apple’s iCloud+ includes Private Relay, which hides your IP address and protects browsing activity primarily in Safari. A full VPN typically protects internet traffic from more apps across the Mac and lets you choose server locations, so a security suite with an included VPN may offer broader privacy and more flexibility.
Identity and dark web monitoring: Some third-party security apps monitor known data breaches and dark web sources for exposed email addresses, passwords and other personal information, then alert you if your details appear in a leak.
Parental controls: Apple’s Screen Time provides app limits, content restrictions, communication controls and family management. Some third-party security suites go a step further by adding more detailed web filtering, activity reporting and cross-platform controls, which can be useful in households with a mix of Macs, PCs and mobile devices.


						

							


What does antivirus not protect you from?
Antivirus software is an essential layer of defense, but it’s not a silver bullet. Antivirus works best alongside good habits: strong passwords, two-factor authentication, cautious clicking, and regular software updates.
Even with antivirus installed you need to be wary of the following: 
Phishing and social engineering scams: Antivirus can sometimes filter out known phishing emails or block malicious links, but it often fails against sophisticated, targeted attacks.
Your own risky behavior: No antivirus can save you if you willingly hand over your password or install software from untrustworthy sources.
Zero-day exploits and advanced threats: While antivirus catches many known threats, it can miss brand-new, never-before-seen attacks (zero-days).
Existing infections and bootkits: Staying updated helps prevent installation, but once a bootkit or similar deep-rooted malware is on your system, antivirus may struggle.
Identity theft and data breaches: Antivirus doesn’t monitor the dark web for your stolen credentials or prevent a company’s database from being hacked. That’s where security suites with dark web monitoring come in.


						

							


Is your Mac still receiving security updates?
Apple typically provides security updates for the three most recent versions of macOS. As of mid-2026, those are macOS Tahoe, macOS Sequoia and macOS Sonoma. When macOS 27 Golden Gate arrives later in 2026, Apple is expected to end security support for Sonoma. 
Macs that can’t run one of Apple’s supported versions will become increasingly vulnerable and may also encounter compatibility problems with websites and apps. 
To check your Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update to see which version of macOS you’re running and whether any updates are available.
Intel Macs are a special case. Apple has confirmed that macOS 27 Golden Gate won’t support Intel-based Macs, but security updates won’t stop immediately. The handful of Intel Macs capable of running macOS Tahoe – including the 2019 16-inch MacBook Pro, 2020 13-inch MacBook Pro, 2020 27-inch iMac and 2019 Mac Pro – are expected to receive security updates until around September 2028.
If your Mac is around a decade old, there’s a good chance it is already running an unsupported version of macOS, in which case upgrading the Mac is a more effective security measure than adding antivirus software.
Antivirus software is no substitute for an operating system that no longer receives security updates.


						

							


How to keep a Mac secure without antivirus
You can keep a Mac quite secure without installing third-party antivirus software by relying on Apple’s built-in protections and practicing good digital hygiene. Here’s how.
Keep macOS updated
This is the single most important step. Apple regularly patches security vulnerabilities through OS updates.

Open System Settings > General > Software Update
Click the i icon beside Automatic Updates
Ensure Install Security Responses and system files is selected
Don’t just stop at macOS – keep browsers and installed apps updated as well.
Only download software from trusted sources
The safest way to get apps is through the Mac App Store, where Apple has vetted the software. If you prefer not to use the App Store, download directly from the developer’s official website. Avoid unfamiliar download sites and never use cracked software, as you will always risk malware exposure.
Be cautious with links and emails
Never open links in emails or texts from unknown or unexpected sources. If a message appears to be from a company you do business with, check the sender’s email address and inspect the URL carefully. You can Control-click a link, select Copy Link Address, and paste it into a text editor to see the actual URL.
Avoid pasting unknown Terminal commands
Attackers sometimes use social engineering to trick users into copying and pasting malicious commands into Terminal. macOS now includes a paste protection feature that warns you when you attempt to paste something into the command line interface. Pay attention to these warnings.
Use strong passwords and passkeys
Create a strong login password – macOS intentionally pauses after a wrong password attempt to discourage brute force attacks.
Enable FileVault
Enable FileVault (full-disk encryption) and the built-in Firewall in System Settings > Network > Firewall.
Check for suspicious activity
If you suspect something is wrong, open Activity Monitor and check the CPU, Network, and Memory tabs for unfamiliar processes consuming excessive resources.
Maintain a current backup
Ensure that if the worst should happen you can wipe your Mac and go back to how things were beforehand with a backup in Time Machine or another Mac backup solution.


						

							


If you do want an antivirus, what should you look for?
When buying antivirus software, the most important thing to remember is that protection quality is the baseline – but the right choice depends on your specific needs, technical comfort level, and budget. Here’s a breakdown of what to prioritize.
Malware Protection Efficacy 
The core job of any antivirus is stopping threats. Look for products that perform well in independent lab tests from organizations like AV-Test and AV-Comparatives, which evaluate detection rates, false positives, and overall protection.
In our tests we recommend options, like Bitdefender and Intego ONE, which we praised for their minimal system impact and fast scan speeds. 
Beware that some options rely on an internet connection to catch threats.
Performance Impact
A good antivirus should protect you without slowing down your Mac. If an app bogs down your Mac, you’ll likely disable it – defeating its purpose. Some suites can be resource hogs during full scans.
Features Beyond Antivirus
Modern security suites bundle a lot of extras. Consider which ones you actually need:

VPN: Unlimited data, multiple protocols, kill switch
Password Manager:Apple has its own password manager, Passwords, but note that this is not cross-platform beyond your Apple products, so if you have non-Apple products you should consider this.
Phishing Protection: Blocks dangerous websites and scam links. Email filtering.
Parental Controls: This will go beyond Apple’s Parental Controls.
Dark Web Monitoring: To track whether your email, phone, credit card appears in breaches.
Ransomware Protection:e.g. Folder locking to protect against ransomware.
Ease of use vs customisation 
The interface should be intuitive. Products like Intego are designed to feel native to macOS, making them particularly easy to navigate.
Some antivirus programs are essentially “cut-back” versions of PC apps. It is often better to choose software specifically tailored for macOS, such as Intego, which is designed to feel native to the platform. Mac-specific tools also tend to integrate better with Apple’s built-in Gatekeeper and XProtect protections.
Beginners should look for simple, set-and-forget interfaces.
Power users will want granular control over settings, whitelists, and network functions.
Lab results
As well as reading our reviews and Best Mac Antivirus recommendations, check how the software performs in tests from AV-Test and V-Comparatives. https://www.macworld.com/article/668850/best-mac-antivirus-software.html
Multiple device coverage
If you have multiple devices, look for plans covering 5–10 devices. Consider how many devices you need to protect. If you have multiple Macs, iPhones, or even Windows PCs, look for “Total Security” or “Family” plans that cover Mac, Windows, Android, and iOS, as these often provide the best overall value.
Subscription Model and Value
Most antivirus software is now subscription-only. Key considerations:
Pricing after the first year/First-year discounts vs. renewal prices: Many products offer steep first-year discounts that jump significantly on renewal.
Free options: Most top-tier antivirus products offer a free trial or a money-back guarantee. This allows you to test the software on your own Mac before committing. Free versions of Avast and AVG are also highly rated.
Ultimately, the best choice depends on your specific needs. If you want the absolute best malware protection and firewall control, Intego ONE is a top pick. If you need a lightweight suite with excellent phishing protection, Avast One is a strong contender. For those who value a powerful VPN alongside antivirus, ESET or Surfshark One+ are worth considering.


						

							





 FAQ 


1.
Does Apple recommend antivirus for Macs?
Apple does not explicitly recommend that every Mac user install third-party antivirus software, but the company has acknowledged that malware on the Mac is a problem. In fact, Apple’s own software engineering chief, Craig Federighi, admitted in 2021 that “We have a level of malware on the Mac that we don’t find acceptable“. 
Instead of issuing a blanket recommendation, Apple has built a robust set of security tools directly into macOS — primarily XProtect and Gatekeeper — which work automatically in the background to block and quarantine known malware. Apple’s protections, while strong, are not bulletproof. While sufficient for low-risk users who stick to the Mac App Store and trusted developers, users who handle sensitive data, frequently download files from various sources, or simply want an extra layer of protection, should consider a dedicated security suite.
Ultimately, Apple’s stance is that its built-in security is a strong baseline, but the decision to add third-party antivirus depends on your personal risk profile.





2.
Is XProtect the same as antivirus?
XProtect is Apple’s built-in antivirus software for macOS. It works automatically in the background to detect, block, and remove known malware without requiring any user configuration.
However, XProtect doesn’t offer continuous, real-time monitoring, only protects against macOS malware (so you could still pass on a Windows virus), is updated less frequently, and lacks additional features only found in third-party solutions.





3.
Do Apple silicon Macs need antivirus?
Apple silicon Macs benefit from a robust, multi-layered security architecture that makes them significantly more resistant to malware than older Intel-based Macs. However, no system is completely invulnerable.
Older Intel Macs are more vulnerable and have a shorter window of security support remaining, making antivirus software a much stronger recommendation for them.





4.
Can antivirus stop phishing attacks?
The short answer is that antivirus software can help, but it is not a silver bullet — especially against newer, psychologically manipulative attacks like ClickFix.
Antivirus can detect phishing attempts. Traditional antivirus suites are quite good at screening for known phishing links and malicious websites. These programs scan your browsing activity, email attachments, and search results for signs of fraud, and they can block access to known dangerous sites. However, phishing attacks are becoming more sophisticated. 
Scammers are increasingly using AI to craft personalized, targeted messages that are much harder for automated filters to catch. In these cases, the human element becomes critical — antivirus alone may not flag a well-crafted, personalized email. 





Macworld’s Recommendation 
Most careful Mac users do not necessarily need third-party antivirus software, because macOS already includes strong built-in protections such as XProtect, Gatekeeper and Notarization.
However, antivirus is worth considering if you regularly download software from unfamiliar sources, handle sensitive business or personal data, share files with Windows users, or want stronger protection against phishing, malicious websites and suspicious downloads. It is also a sensible choice for less technical users or anyone who wants an additional safety net. 
Whatever you decide, antivirus should complement rather than replace good security habits, including keeping macOS up to date, using strong passwords and MFA, and avoiding suspicious links, downloads and Terminal commands.

title: iPhone 18 Pro pre-orders might start later than usual this year
content:
Macworld





Just a few days ago, Apple announced the date for its annual Phone event: Wednesday, September 9, less than two weeks away. We’re expecting Apple to unveil its first-ever folding iPhone at the event, along with the iPhone 18 Pro and Apple Watch Series 12. But if you’re looking to buy one of them, you might have to wait longer than usual.
A reliable source has told Macwelt that pre-orders this year are not set to begin, as usual, on the Friday following the launch. Instead, Apple will open pre-orders a day later, on Saturday, September 12. The reason for this is that this year, September 11 falls on the Friday following the event, a day of remembrance and mourning in the U.S.
The time is also set to change, according to the source: While pre-orders usually begin at 5 am PT, Apple is reportedly opening up pre-sales at midnight PT on Saturday.
It wouldn’t be the first time Apple has moved pre-orders from Friday to the following Saturday: 11 years ago, the iPhone 6S and 6S Plus weren’t available for pre-order until Saturday, September 12, 2015, for the same reason. 
This preorder should apply to the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and any other surprises Apple has in store. However, if you’re looking to buy one of the foldable iPhone Ultras, reports claim that preorders might not begin until late September. A similar situation occurred in 2020, when the iPhone 12 Mini and the iPhone 12 Pro Max were launched later than the iPhone 12 and the iPhone 12 Pro due to the coronavirus pandemic. Apple also delayed the iPhone X in 2017 due to production issues with the next-gen handset.

title: Apple is making it really difficult to buy its highest-end Mac Studio
content:
Macworld





Earlier this week, Apple surprised us with a brand-new Mac Studio powered by an M5 Ultra processor and up to 512GB of RAM. We expect that option, which won’t be available until late October, will cost upwards of $15,000.
That in itself will limit its availability to a very small percentage of Mac users. So the people who try to buy one will be a very small group.
It would stand to reason that people in that small group would be perfect candidates for Apple’s new Upgrade program, which lets you lease Macs for either 24 or 36 months and then upgrade to a new model once all payments have been made. However, Apple and Klarna, the financial partner for the program, have seemingly set up nearly impossible terms for qualification.
There are numerous social media reports of people who have been declined for M5 Ultra Mac Studio leases, so I tried to get one and failed several times, with the following message:
Klarna could not approve your application.
Thank you for your interest in Apple Upgrade. Klarna was unable to approve your application at this time. Details about this decision will be sent to the email registered with your Klarna account. Your order wasn’t placed and you haven’t been charged.
If you’d still like to proceed with your order, you can continue shopping with a different payment option. Your device selections have been saved, but you may need to make a few of your decisions again.
I was also denied a lease for a fully decked-out 16-inch MacBook Pro, so it’s not limited to the Mac Studio. It just be noted that it’s been several hours and I haven’t received an email with any more details from Klarna.
It’s unclear why the system seems to be denying purchases of $10,000 or more. Klarna doesn’t run a credit check, and approvals are often made within seconds for iPhones or iPads. But if you’re looking to lease a very expensive Mac, you might be out of luck.

title: AirPods: Here are the new features in iOS 27
content:
Macworld





Arguably the greatest feat of the AirPods is that they gain new features with every iOS update without the need for any hardware changes: in 2024, they became (rudimentary) hearing aids, and with iOS 26 came live translation. So it’s hardly surprising that the AirPods will also gain new features with iOS 27, for which you won’t need to buy new headphones.
If you’d like, you can try out these features right now with the iOS 27 beta – or you can wait about another month until iOS 27 is released to everyone.
iOS 27: All the new AirPods features
Equaliser
Perhaps it’s because Apple met with a lot of discontent over the new sound profile of the AirPods Pro 3, or perhaps it was simply about time: with iOS 27, Apple is finally giving AirPods an equalizer. Of course, you shouldn’t expect a comprehensive 7-band equalizer like those from other manufacturers, but the three frequency ranges that Apple allows you to adjust are better than nothing.
The equalizer requires the H2 chip and is therefore available on the AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Pro 3, AirPods 4, and AirPods Max 2. You’ll find it under Settings > [Name of your AirPods] > Audio & Routing > Equalizer.
Revised settings
When you go to the AirPods settings to access the equalizer, you may notice a few changes. Whilst this section previously consisted of a more or less random list of functions and settings, Apple has tidied it up properly in iOS 27. The various settings are now logically grouped into subcategories and are therefore much clearer.

While we’re on the subject of settings: With iOS 27, Apple is expanding the AirPods’ noise-cancelling settings. If you use Adaptive Mode, which dynamically adjusts active noise cancellation depending on ambient noise, you can now set it to operate closer to Transparency Mode or to Noise Cancellation.
There’s a new interface for this, both in the ‘Hearing Mode’ section of Settings and in the Control Center. When the middle icon – Adaptive Mode – is selected, a new slider appears between the two outer icons – Transparency Mode on the left and Noise Cancellation on the right – a new slider, which allows you to move the Adaptive Mode icon across several levels and thus adjust its starting point in one direction or the other.
In the Control Center, with your AirPods connected, you need to press and hold the volume indicator for a few seconds and then tap the Listening Mode icon in the bottom left-hand corner to bring up the mode selection. Accessibility – Name Recognition
If you use your AirPods as a hearing aid, iOS 27 introduces a new feature: if your AirPods detect that someone is calling your name, you’ll receive a notification to alert you to this. You can enable this feature using a toggle under Settings > Accessibility > Sound & Name Detection (in the ‘Hearing’ section).
Siri AI
As soon as the new Siri AI is available, you’ll be able to speak to the new version just as you do with the old one. This works much better, as Siri AI now also understands natural language.
The downside: At present, Siri AI only understands English. And for regulatory reasons, it currently only runs on Mac and Apple TV within the EU. It is not yet known when Siri AI will also be available on the iPhone and iPad in the EU, as the European Commission refers to Apple as a ‘gatekeeper’ due to its market power.

title: Watch out for this fake Face ID Apple Pay pop-up scam
content:
Macworld





The security, antivirus, and VPN company Malwarebytes has an interesting post on its Malwarebytes Labs blog detailing a new and sophisticated scam.
The web-based trick is meant to make users think that they just made a big payment with Apple Pay, with the goal being to trick them into calling a fake “Apple Support” number. That’s the real objective: Once they have you talking to a fake support agent, they’ll gather personal or financial info to actually take your money.
How it works
The scam uses a variety of web technologies to make it look, to the untrained eye, like an Apple Pay charge for $657 to the App Store has been made. There’s a fake Face ID animation, a padlock unlocking, a transaction ID, and a host of other cues that can fool many users into thinking the charge is real.
It then pops up a receipt and shows a large phone number to “call Apple Support” along with a View Details button.  If the user taps the button, the web page plays an audio voice alert that says: “Unauthorized charge of six hundred fifty-seven dollars from your Apple ID. Please call support immediately.”
It’s all fake. It’s just web-based images, animations, and sounds. The amount and transaction ID are the same for everyone, and there was never any Face ID check or transaction attempted at all. The goal is to get the user to think that a big unauthorized charge was made, panic, and to call the fake Apple Support number.
If you try to hit the back button on your browser, a warning pops up that claims your “Apple ID session is active” (which isn’t a thing) and that leaving the page could expose your payments and banking info to serious threats. All of that is, of course, false.
Never call a popup number
If you happen to be on a web page and see this scam, the best thing you can do is open the tab view in your browser (the bottom-right button on Safari) and close the tab entirely.
Don’t tap on any of the dialog boxes or interface elements and definitely do not call the number.
As a matter of course, you should never dial a number in a popup or sent to you in a text message. No legitimate company will ever make a popup message with a phone number for you to call, and they will not text you a phone number unless you’re already in the middle of a support process with them and are expecting it.

title: Tim Cook wasn’t Steve Jobs. He was better
content:
Macworld





The clock is ticking; in just a few days, Tim Cook’s 15-year tenure as Apple CEO will come to an end. Looking back at the past decade and a half, I’d distill the company’s progress into a couple of words: growth and stability. Cook may not be perceived as iconic or innovative as Steve Jobs, but he was undoubtedly the perfect pick to lead Apple after his death. And he may go down as the best CEO Apple has ever had.
Back in 2011, Apple needed a mastermind who would further establish it as a leading tech brand, grow its customer base and value, and prepare it for the next phase. Tim Cook did exactly that, building upon Steve’s legacy, strengthening Apple’s structure, and forging new paths for the future. 
Inheriting the empire
Succeeding Steve Jobs is a challenge in itself. Apple enthusiasts and shareholders naturally had high expectations, leaving Tim Cook little room for error. Despite that, Cook cooked, as the kids say. Not only did he launch a wide array of budget-friendly products, but Tim also maintained Apple’s overall image as a premium brand that sells high-quality, carefully crafted devices. Apple’s attention to detail lives on, and so do its trendsetting designs.
When Tim took over in 2011, Apple’s market value was around $337 billion, nothing to scoff at. Today, the company is worth around $4.5 trillion, a whopping 13.5-fold increase that has crowned it as one of the world’s most valuable companies. It now also makes over 4x more in annual revenue, and the number of active Apple devices has risen from 200 million to over 2.5 billion—a 14x increase over 15 years.
Catering to more than a billion unique customers comes with lots of hurdles, including geopolitical ones. During his time as CEO, Cook expanded manufacturing to new countries, such as India and Vietnam, reducing Apple’s reliance on China. He also maintained lower product pricing for longer than Apple’s competitors during the current memory crisis.
Transforming existing devices
It might seem like an easy task to take over the reins of Apple after the iPhone and iPad had already been launched, but in fact, it’s quite the opposite. Cook had to juggle numerous products in their infancy while fending off competitors and giving users reasons to upgrade every year.

				
					

				
			
At the time, the iPhone 6 was a major step toward Apple’s move into larger iPhones.

Apple




iPhone
Steve Jobs may have created the iPhone, but Tim Cook reimagined it. The iPhone’s overall design had persisted until Cook unveiled the iPhone 6 and 6 Plus in 2014, barely three years after he had taken over. This move helped popularize larger smartphones and prepared the handset for a future dominated by digital media. A few generations later, the iPhone X debuted, completely overhauling the iPhone’s design and courageously retiring the iconic physical Home button in favor of gesture navigation. Then the first iPhone Pro followed a couple of years later, providing power users with an even more premium mobile computing experience.
Tim Cook didn’t just lead the iPhone design evolution, but he also helped make the product more accessible. He first experimented with the iPhone 5c and learned from its shortcomings what customers expect from an affordable Apple device. He then refined the formula with the SE line accordingly and perfected it with the latest “e” editions. We’ve now reached a point where there’s an iPhone for everyone.
iPad
The iPad was barely a year old when Tim Cook took over as CEO. During his tenure, Apple’s tablet grew in leaps and bounds and saw some of its most significant developments yet. He introduced the mini, Air, and Pro models, giving users several sizes and an array of features to pick from. He also oversaw the release of the Apple Pencil and Magic Keyboard, which turned the tablet into a serious productivity device. Coupled with the maturity of iPadOS, many users can now depend on an iPad to get professional work done. It’s no longer the plus-sized, constrained iPhone it used to be in 2011.
Mac
The Mac also saw unprecedented gains during Cook’s leadership. Like iPhones and iPads, he expanded the line, but more importantly, he oversaw the transition from Intel to Apple’s own M-series chips, hands down the Mac’s most transformative evolution of the past decade. This has enabled Apple to shrink its computers, boost their speeds, and make them more power-efficient than ever.
When Tim Cook took over Apple, it had only just launched its first in-house system-on-chip, the A4, in the original iPad and iPhone 4 a year before. Now that iPhones, iPads, and Macs are powered by comparable Apple silicon chips, the company has been able to repurpose some of its processors across the lineup. High-end iPads pack Mac chips, while the affordable MacBook Neo is powered by the same brain as an iPhone.
Launching new products
Tim Cook isn’t always associated with innovative new products, but several iconic products launched during his time as CEO, expanding Apple’s portfolio into new categories and shaping an ecosystem no other company has.

				
					

				
			
Tim Cook’s first new product was the Apple Watch, and it was an enormous hit.

Apple




Apple Watch
Beyond refining existing products, Tim Cook launched all-new device categories that reshaped their respective industries. The Apple Watch has become the most popular smartwatch on the planet and the go-to recommendation for most casual users. Today, Apple sells three main models with several different sizes, materials, and price points, suitable for a wide array of users and uses, from everyday casual wear to extreme athletes. It’s not just the most popular smartwatch—it’s the most popular watch brand in the world.
AirPods
Likewise, AirPods popularized wireless earbuds and have remarkably evolved over the years. When Apple removed the headphone jack from the iPhone 7 and launched the original AirPods, there was a small revolt among Apple fans who didn’t like the design or the direction. But Tim stuck to his vision, and years later, AirPods are as iconic as the iPhone itself, with an array of models and features that support advanced audio features, hearing health tools, heartbeat monitoring, and much more.
Services
Cook hasn’t been solely focused on Apple hardware. He also launched several subscription services that now contribute to the company’s revenue and rival established names in the field, including Apple Music, TV+, Arcade, News+, Fitness+, Creator Studio, and more. 
But the biggest contribution of Tim’s Services push is Apple Pay. Announced in 2014, it pushed niche contactless payments into the mainstream and transformed the way we purchase just about everything. A few years later, Apple Card solidified Apple’s place as a leader in the digital finance realm, and today it’s rare to find a vendor that doesn’t support Apple Pay.

				
					

				
			
Apple Music kicked off a push into services that turned subscriptions into one of Apple’s biggest revenue streams. 

Apple




Laying a foundation for the future
While Tim Cook will no longer be Apple’s CEO, he has already planted several seeds that are set to kickstart the John Ternus era. The Vision Pro, for example, may not be the company’s most well-received product, but the technology it packs prepares for a future of lighter smart-glasses and spatial computing devices.
After a bumpy road to the start of Apple Intelligence, it’s set to get on firmer footing with the launch of the new Siri AI as part of iOS 27. It will officially arrive during Ternus’ first few weeks, but its solid, private foundation is one of Cook’s most important final projects.
Other seeds may start to bloom on September 9. During its upcoming event, Apple will reportedly launch the iPhone Ultra, its first foldable device. A touchscreen MacBook Ultra could follow soon after, possibly followed by Ultra versions of AirPods and folding iPads down the road. Revitalizing the Ultra branding signals a dramatic shift in Apple’s philosophy and suggests a shift is around the corner. 
Incoming CEO John Ternus will announce these products, but they will all contribute to Tim Cook’s lasting impact at the company that he led to greatness. Tim Cook will never supplant Steve Jobs as the face of Apple, but Cook’s legacy will be almost impossible to top.

title: Tim Cook Stepping Down as Apple CEO Next Week: 15 Years in Quotes
content:
Tim Cook will be stepping down as Apple's CEO in just five more days, with the company's hardware engineering chief John Ternus set to take over.


Below, we have surfaced some of Cook's notable quotes over his 15 years leading Apple.

I want you to be confident that Apple is not going to change. I cherish and celebrate Apple's unique principles and values. Steve built a company and culture that is unlike any other in the world and we are going to stay true to that - it is in our DNA. We are going to continue to make the best products in the world that delight our customers and make our employees incredibly proud of what they do.
May 2012, on Apple's secrecy:
We're going to double down on secrecy on products. I'm serious.
September 2012, in a public apology about the botched launch of Apple Maps:
At Apple, we strive to make world-class products that deliver the best experience possible to our customers. With the launch of our new Maps last week, we fell short on this commitment. We are extremely sorry for the frustration this has caused our customers and we are doing everything we can to make Maps better.
December 2012, when asked if it is true that he wakes up at 3:45 a.m. every morning:
Yes, every morning.
The thing about it is, when you love what you do, you don't really think of it as work. It's what you do. And that's the good fortune of where I find myself.
October 2014, in a public essay:
I'm proud to be gay, and I consider being gay among the greatest gifts God has given me.
March 2015, the month before the Apple Watch launched:
Apple Watch begins a new chapter in the way we relate to technology and we think our customers are going to love it. We can't wait for people to start wearing Apple Watch to easily access information that matters, to interact with the world, and to live a better day by being more aware of their daily activity than ever before.
October 2015, on privacy:
We see that privacy is a fundamental human right that people have.
June 2017, expressing his excitement about augmented reality:
I think it is profound. I am so excited about it, I just want to yell out and scream.
March 2018, on what he would do if he were Mark Zuckerberg, amid a Facebook privacy scandal:
I wouldn't be in this situation.
March 2020, in response to COVID-19:
There is no mistaking the challenge of this moment. The entire Apple family is indebted to the heroic first responders, doctors, nurses, researchers, public health experts and public servants globally who have given every ounce of their spirit to help the world meet this moment.
August 2022, on Apple's legacy:
I think that when we look back one day and ask, what's been Apple's greatest contribution, it will be in health.
September 2022, in response to a customer asking why the iPhone did not support RCS, when Android smartphones already did at the time:
Buy your mom an iPhone.
June 2023, in Apple's Vision Pro announcement:
Today marks the beginning of a new era for computing. Just as the Mac introduced us to personal computing, and iPhone introduced us to mobile computing, Apple Vision Pro introduces us to spatial computing. Built upon decades of Apple innovation, Vision Pro is years ahead and unlike anything created before — with a revolutionary new input system and thousands of groundbreaking innovations.
April 2026, upon announcing he is stepping down as CEO:
It has been the greatest privilege of my life to be the CEO of Apple and to have been trusted to lead such an extraordinary company. I love Apple with all of my being, and I am so grateful to have had the opportunity to work with a team of such ingenious, innovative, creative, and deeply caring people who have been unwavering in their dedication to enriching the lives of our customers and creating the best products and services in the world.
And a list of Cook quotes would not be complete without:
Good moooorning!
Cook will remain at Apple as executive chairman on the company's board of directors. In this role, Apple said he will "assist with certain aspects of the company, including engaging with policymakers around the world."

title: 2025 vs. 2026 Mac Studio Buyer's Guide: All Upgrades Compared
content:
Apple this week announced a new Mac Studio with the M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips, discontinuing the M4 Max and M3 Ultra models that had been on sale since March 2025.


The machine's design is unchanged for a fifth consecutive year, with all of the upgrades being internal. The table below details everything that changed regardless of whether you choose a Max or an Ultra chip. The two tables that follow break down the differences within each tier.

What Changed Across Both Models

Here's everything that differs between the 2025 and 2026 ‌Mac Studio‌ irrespective of configuration:







‌Mac Studio‌ (2025)
‌Mac Studio‌ (2026)


Baseline SSD read and write speeds
Next-generation SSD architecture built on PCIe Gen 6, with up to twice the read and write speeds


Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax)
Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) via the Apple-designed N1 chip


Bluetooth 5.3
Bluetooth 6



Genlock over USB-C




iPhone 17 lineup. Apple also says the new machine is made with 35% recycled content overall, including 100% recycled aluminum in the enclosure and 100% recycled rare earth elements in all magnets.

Mac Studio M4 Max vs. M5 Max

Here's everything that differs between the M4 Max and M5 Max configurations:







‌Mac Studio‌ (M4 Max, 2025)
‌Mac Studio‌ (M5 Max, 2026)


M4 Max chip
M5 Max chip


14-core CPU, configurable to 16-core, with 12 performance cores and 4 efficiency cores
18-core CPU with 6 super cores and 12 performance cores


32-core GPU, configurable to 40-core
32-core GPU, configurable to 40-core, with Neural Accelerators built into every core and enhanced shader cores


Second-generation hardware-accelerated ray tracing
Third-generation hardware-accelerated ray tracing


Up to 546GB/s memory bandwidth
Up to 614GB/s memory bandwidth


36GB unified memory with the 32-core GPU, or 64GB with the 40-core GPU (128GB option withdrawn in May 2026)
36GB unified memory with the 32-core GPU, or 48GB, 64GB, or 128GB with the 40-core GPU


Weighs 6.1 pounds (2.74 kg)
Weighs 6.0 pounds (2.7 kg)


Now discontinued
Starts at $2,499




The most immediately useful change is at the entry level. The M4 Max started with a 14-core CPU and could be configured up to 16 cores, whereas the M5 Max has an 18-core CPU as standard with no CPU upgrade to buy. Apple has also changed its core architecture, dropping the performance and efficiency split in favor of 6 super cores and 12 performance cores.

Mac Studio M3 Ultra vs. M5 Ultra

The table below outlines every difference between the two Ultra configurations:







‌Mac Studio‌ (M3 Ultra, 2025)
‌Mac Studio‌ (M5 Ultra, 2026)


M3 Ultra chip
M5 Ultra chip


28-core CPU, configurable to 32-core, with 24 performance cores and 8 efficiency cores
30-core CPU, configurable to 36-core, with 12 super cores and 24 performance cores


60-core GPU, configurable to 80-core
64-core GPU, configurable to 80-core, with Neural Accelerators built into every core and enhanced shader cores


First-generation hardware-accelerated ray tracing
Third-generation hardware-accelerated ray tracing


Dynamic Caching
Second-generation Dynamic Caching


819GB/s memory bandwidth
1.2TB/s memory bandwidth


96GB, 256GB, or 512GB unified memory (512GB option withdrawn in March 2026 and the 256GB option withdrawn in May 2026)
96GB or 256GB unified memory, or 512GB with the 80-core GPU


Now discontinued
Starts at $5,499




Across both generations, the maximum GPU still contains 80 cores, the Neural Engine still contains 32 cores, display support and media engine is identical, storage still maxes out at 16TB, and maximum unified memory is still 512GB. The 1.2TB/s of bandwidth feeding that memory, which is 50% higher than before, and the Neural Accelerators for each GPU core, are among the key changes.

How Big Are the Upgrades?

Apple's own comparisons against the outgoing chips are heavily weighted toward AI and graphics. For the M5 Max against the M4 Max, Apple claims:


Up to 3.9x faster LLM prompt processing in LM Studio

Up to 3.5x faster text-to-image performance

Up to 3x faster Magic Mask performance in Blackmagic Design DaVinci Resolve Studio

Up to 1.9x faster basecalling for DNA sequencing in Oxford Nanopore MinKNOW

Up to 50% faster graphics performance



For the M5 Ultra against the M3 Ultra, Apple claims:


Up to 4.3x faster text-to-image performance

Up to 4x faster LLM prompt processing in LM Studio

Up to 3.3x faster CopyCat ML training performance in Foundry Nuke

Up to 1.8x faster graphics performance

Up to 1.7x faster scene rendering performance in Maxon Redshift

Up to 1.3x higher multithreaded CPU performance



On either chip, tasks that use matrix multiplication can run three to four times faster thanks to new Neural Accelerators in each GPU core.

Which to Choose?

Apple no longer sells the M4 Max or M3 Ultra models, which became relatively poor value for money by the end of their run. The M4 Max cost $2,499 with a 14-core CPU and up to 64GB of memory. For the same price, the M5 Max has an 18-core CPU, 614GB/s memory bandwidth, up to 128GB of memory, twice-fast storage, and Wi‑Fi 7. The M3 Ultra ended at $5,299 with a 96GB memory limit. For $200 more, the M5 Ultra brings back 256GB and 512GB options and adds 50% more memory bandwidth.

Current M4 Max and M3 Ultra owners generally do not need to upgrade after only 17 months. Launch buyers paid $1,999 or $3,999, so replacing their machine now costs 25–38% more for the same design, ports, Ultra core limits, storage limit, and Media Engine. The main exception is AI-heavy work. Local LLMs, on-device image or video generation, and demanding machine-learning tasks in applications like DaVinci Resolve or Nuke can benefit substantially from the new Neural Accelerators. The M5 Ultra's 1.2TB/s memory bandwidth can also improve large-model token generation.

M1 or M2 ‌Mac Studio‌ owners. Apple says the M5 Max can process prompts up to 10.7× faster than the M1 Max, while the M5 Ultra can train ML models up to 15.4× faster than the M1 Ultra. Older models also lack Thunderbolt 5, AV1 decoding, and the newer Media Engine. If you already skipped the 2025 refresh, this is a more meaningful step forward.

The 2025 models are mainly worth considering used or refurbished at a steep discount. Apple raised prices in June, so lightly discounted older stock is often too close in price to a new model. One notable exception is an M3 Ultra with 256GB or 512GB of memory, since those configurations were unavailable new for much of 2026 and M5 Ultra equivalents will not ship until later this year.

late October, with pricing expected to start above $10,000.

discontinued the Mac Pro in March, seemingly with no plans for a replacement. There is no higher end Mac to wait for and no internal expansion path beyond adding a second machine.

title: Apple Event: Six New Products to Expect on September 9
content:
Apple has announced that it will be holding an event on Wednesday, September 9 at 10 a.m. Pacific Time, with the company widely expected to unveil the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, its first-ever foldable iPhone, and more.


Other products expected to be announced at the event include an Apple Watch Series 12 with a ceramic case option, an Apple Watch Ultra 4, AirPods 5 with and without active noise cancellation, and potentially more.

Here are the six products most likely to be unveiled at the event.

Most Likely


iPhone 18 Pro: A20 Pro chip, a smaller Dynamic Island, a simplified Camera Control button, a Dark Cherry color option, and more.

iPhone 18 Pro Max: The same features rumored for the iPhone 18 Pro, but the Pro Max model may be slightly thicker due to a larger battery and a variable aperture camera, which might be exclusive to the Pro Max model this year.

iPhone Ultra: A foldable iPhone Ultra with a 7.7-inch inner display and 5.3-inch outer display, two rear cameras, one front camera, a Touch ID power button instead of Face ID, and more. iOS 27 is expected to be tailored for the foldable iPhone, allowing for side-by-side apps and other iPad-like multitasking functionality.

Apple Watch Series 12: A faster S11 chip or newer, longer battery life, fitness tracking improvements, and a ceramic case option.

Apple Watch Ultra 4: A faster S11 chip or newer, fitness tracking improvements, and additional satellite features for the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and newer, such as Apple Maps via satellite and the ability to send and receive photos with Messages via satellite. Touch ID was initially rumored, but seemingly ruled out.
AirPods 5: Two new AirPods 5 models with and without active noise cancellation.

Other Possibilities


Many of the products below are more likely to be announced in October this year, but perhaps some of them will appear at the September event.

iPad mini: A19 Pro or A20 Pro chip, an OLED display, a vibration-based speaker system, and a water-resistant design.

iMac: M6 chip and new color options.

14-inch MacBook Pro: A new 14-inch MacBook Pro base model with an M6 chip.

MacBook Ultra: A major MacBook Pro redesign in late 2026 or early 2027, with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, an OLED display, a touch screen, a Dynamic Island, and a thinner design. On this laptop, which will reportedly be named MacBook Ultra, macOS 27 is expected to offer a touch-friendly interface.

Apple TV: At least five new features, including an A17 Pro chip or newer, an increased 8GB of RAM for Apple Intelligence, Siri AI support, an Apple-designed N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 support, and an updated Siri Remote.

HomePod mini: Newer chip with Siri AI support, improved sound quality, Apple's N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 support, a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip, and potentially new color options like red.

Home Hub: An all-new smart home hub featuring Siri AI, a 6-inch to 7-inch square display, an A18 chip for Apple Intelligence, FaceTime, and more. There will a tabletop version with a speaker base and a wall-mounted version.

title: If you ordered an M4 Mac mini, you may be getting a free M6 upgrade
content:
Macworld





Apple surprised us all by announcing a new Mac mini this week with an M6 processor and a higher price tag than the comparable M4 model it replaces. But if you’re one of the lucky people who had ordered one ahead of the announcement, you might be in line for a free upgrade.
The M4 Mac mini had been backordered for months, so this new model will hopefully offer some relief. While it’s not available until September 22, Apple’s online ordering system still guarantees you’ll get it on that date, even with the highest memory and storage options. That’s about a month earlier than some of the longest estimates for the previous M4 model.
So naturally, anyone who had an M4 on backorder would want to upgrade to the new model. The good news is you don’t have to—Apple is already doing it for you.
Numerous accounts on social media have shared an email from Apple regarding their M4 Mac mini orders:
Thank you for your recent Mac order. We know you’re looking forward to receiving your purchase.
As you may know, Apple recently announced the new Mac mini. Since your order has yet to ship, we automatically upgraded you to the new Mac mini at no additional cost.
The “no additional cost” bit is important. With the M6 Mac mini, Apple has raised prices by $100, so these buyers are essentially getting a $100 discount on a new M6. Not only will the machine be much faster, but it’ll also be a better value.
It’s not clear how far Apple is going back to offer upgrades. The usual policy is to offer refunds within a 14-day period, but some purchases have been backordered for much longer. So if you have an M4 on backorder and haven’t heard from Apple, reach out to the store. They may have a surprise waiting for you.

title: iOS 27 finally lets you separately adjust the volume of ringtones, alarms, and alerts
content:
Macworld





It’s one of the more persistently annoying aspects of owning an iPhone, and one of those dumb little things where Apple was overzealous in making things simple and left us with a frustration that most Android users haven’t had to deal with for years: Independent volume controls for various kinds of system sounds.
Sure, you’ve been able to adjust the volume for media (videos or music) separately from system sounds for ages. But there’s been one “Ringtone and Alerts” volume setting that controls everything else. Turn it up so your phone rings loudly, your timers will blast your ears off, and your alarm going off on your bedside table will make you jump out of bed. Lower it, and you risk sleeping through a wake-up call.
Now, at long last, Apple is giving us the ability to set independent volumes for different sounds. iOS 27 splits these sounds into three groups: Ringtones, Alarms and Timers, and Alerts and System Sounds.

				
					

				
			In iOS 26 (left) you have one system volume. In iOS 27, Apple lets you split it into three, if you want.
Foundry




Controlling these volume settings independently is easy and optional. Here’s where you find it:
Open Settings
Tap Sound & Haptics
Tap Match Ringtone Volume under Alarms and Timers or Alerts and System Sounds, as desired.
This will make a volume slider appear. Sounds will play as you adjust it, so you can hear how long or soft it is.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




If you like the simplicity of fewer volumes to adjust, you can simply leave the “Match Ringtone volume” switched on. So iOS 27 gives you to option to independently adjust just the type of system sounds you want. 
Adjusting the volume with your volume buttons when listening to media or on a call will continue to adjust the volume of just media or calls, the same way iOS has worked for years.

title: 6 Mac mini and Mac Studio upgrades you may have missed
content:
Macworld





Apple just announced the new M6 / M5 Pro Mac mini and M5 Max/Ultra Mac Studio, both of which are shipping on September 22. On the surface, these look like just the same Macs we have today with faster processors inside. But there’s more to them if you dig a little deeper.
Apple promotes these machines with nonspecific performance incremental values: 4.3x faster AI performance, 2x faster graphics, 4.8x faster LLM prompt performance, and so on. All of those claims will have to wait until we can do real testing with real applications. But while the outside of the Macs hasn’t changed, there are a number of features and differences you may have glossed over. Here are some of the more interesting differences between these new Macs and their predecessors.
Faster storage: Both the new Mac minis and Mac Studios feature SSDs using the new PCIe Gen 6 standard, with speeds up to twice as fast. Storage performance is a bottleneck to overall system responsiveness more often than you think, so this should really make a difference.
Upgraded Ethernet: The Mac mini used to come with a standard gigabit Ethernet port; that has now been upgraded to a 2.5Gb port. The 10Gb port upgrade option is still there, while the Mac Studio still comes with a 10Gb port standard.
Better wireless: Both systems now feature Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, up from the Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3 of their predecessors.
Genlock support: Both the Mac mini and Mac Studio now support Genlock over USB-C, a special timing signal standard used to keep multi-camera video shoots in sync. It won’t matter to most users, but if you’re someone who uses it, it’ll cut down on extra equipment.
Dual Neural Engines: Apple’s chips have had a 16-core Neural Engine for some time now. But what’s better than one 16-core Neural Engine? Two! So the M6 has two 16-core Neural Engines. All the M5 chips still have one, including the M5 Ultra, though since it’s two M5 Max chips interconnected, it has a “32-core” Neural Engine, just like the M3 Ultra.
Higher refresh rates: In three- and four-monitor configurations, the M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini supports higher refresh rates. With three displays, the 4K resolution used to be capped at 60Hz; now it’s up to 165Hz for the two displays connected via Thunderbolt. The M5 Pro version can run three 4K displays at 165 Hz, while the M4 Pro was limited to 60Hz. For a single display, refresh rates are unchanged: 8K at 60Hz, 5K at 120Hz, or 4K at 240Hz.

The percentage change in price of a product as impacted by rapidly rising prices in RAM and Storage isn’t purely depending on the discrete amount of each. 
Rather, it depends on the percentage of that product’s cost that is tied to those components. A product not having much RAM or Storage may mean you’ll see a smaller discrete change in cost but not a smaller percentage change. 
In the Apple TV’s case, what RAM and Storage it DOES have makes up a large portion of the product’s price already. 
It doesn’t have an expensive display or camera module to mask the cost of components like storage and RAM. As a result, if the RAM and Storage rises in cost, it has a much larger impact on the overall cost of the product. 
This is to say, it makes PERFECT sense why the Apple TV would see such a large percentage change in price with the increased price of RAM and storage. 
If there are products you’d EXPECT to see that level of change, it’s products like the Apple TV and the Mac Studio.

Open Finder and choose Go, then Home, or press Shift-Command-H.
